## Common Collocations
- **darse cuenta de (que)** — to realize; always reflexive, always with **de**
- **resulta que** — it turns out that; used to introduce surprising information
- **de repente** — suddenly; signals a preterite action interrupting an imperfect background
- **había una vez** — once upon a time; classic story opener (imperfect of **haber**)
- **lo que pasó fue que** — what happened was; long but natural way to start explaining
- **al final de cuentas** — at the end of the day / when all is said and done
- **pasar de todo** — for everything to happen; "Nos pasó de todo" = "Everything happened to us"
- **contar una historia** — to tell a story; uses **contar**, not **decir**

## False Cognates and Tricky Translations
- **la historia** vs **history/story**: **Historia** means both "history" and "story." Context determines which. A fictional story is more precisely **un cuento** (short) or **una novela** (long).
- **actualmente** vs **actually**: **Actualmente** means "currently." Actually is **de hecho**, **en realidad**, or **la verdad es que**.
- **realizar** vs **realize**: **Realizar** means to carry out / accomplish. To realize (become aware) is **darse cuenta de**.
- **suceder** vs **succeed**: **Suceder** means to happen. To succeed is **tener éxito** or **lograr**.

## Dialect Variations
- **suddenly**: **de repente** is universal. Mexico also uses **de pronto** and colloquially **de volada** (slang).
- **to tell a story**: **contar** is universal. **Platicar** (Mexico) can mean to tell/narrate casually.
- **once upon a time**: **Había una vez** is standard. Some regions also use **Érase una vez** (Spain, more literary).
- **it turns out**: **resulta que** is universal. **Sale que** is colloquial in some regions.

## Cultural and Pragmatic Notes
- **Preterite/imperfect as storytelling tools**: Storytelling is the most natural context for preterite vs. imperfect contrast. Imperfect sets the scene ("Era de noche, llovía..."), preterite advances the action ("De repente, alguien gritó"). This cluster reinforces B-04 through authentic narrative practice.
- **Narrative filler words**: Spanish storytellers use **entonces**, **pues**, **bueno**, **y luego** as natural fillers while thinking. These are not errors — they're discourse markers that signal "I'm still talking."
- **Storytelling as social bonding**: Sharing personal anecdotes (**anécdotas**) is a major social activity in Spanish-speaking cultures. Stories tend to be longer and more detailed than typical English small talk. Interrupting a story to ask questions or react is expected and appreciated.
- **"Lo + adjective" pattern**: **Lo bueno**, **lo malo**, **lo increíble**, **lo curioso** — this neuter article pattern is highly productive for storytelling. It nominalizes adjectives: "the good thing," "the incredible part."

## Pronunciation Alerts
- **desenlace** — stress on the third syllable: de-sen-LA-ce. Not de-SEN-la-ce.
- **anécdota** — esdrújula: a-NÉC-do-ta. English speakers tend to stress the first syllable.
- **protagonista** — stress on the fourth syllable: pro-ta-go-NIS-ta.
- **mientras** — two syllables: MIEN-tras. Don't add a third syllable.
- **entonces** — three syllables: en-TON-ces. The final **-es** is not a separate stressed syllable.
